SignalRank: Predicting Which News Events Will Matter from Their First Hour of Coverage

DATA 226 Group Project · Team 10 · Fall 2026
Sreeram Achutuni  ·  Dev Dhiren Faldu  ·  Pranav Sharma
Abstract. Newsrooms, analysts and risk teams face thousands of new events every hour and must decide early which ones deserve attention. We study whether the first hour of global media coverage can predict which events will keep spreading. Using 2,304 15-minute files of the GDELT 2.0 Events, Mentions and Global Knowledge Graph tables for 20–27 October 2026 (11.5 GB uncompressed; 0.86 M events, 2.3 M mentions, 0.8 M articles) we build a Spark batch pipeline, a Kafka + Structured Streaming scorer, an MLflow-tracked model comparison, a FastAPI service and a Streamlit dashboard. An event "matters" if at least 3 publishers that were not covering it in hour one pick it up during the next 48 hours (6.6% of training events). A gradient-boosted-tree model that adds a leakage-safe publisher-reach prior reaches PR-AUC 0.585 and F1 0.569 on a held-out weekend, versus 0.474 and 0.512 for the best simple rule (count first-hour publishers); the gains (+0.111 PR-AUC, +0.057 F1) are well outside bootstrap intervals. Streaming and batch scoring agree exactly on 12,202 replayed events. We also quantify a hard limit: 39% of the events that matter start with a single publisher and are almost undetectable at hour one.
Keywords: GDELT, news-event importance, early prediction, Spark MLlib, Structured Streaming, MLflow, model serving

1  Introduction

Every 15 minutes GDELT publishes thousands of newly coded events from news around the world. Most are routine: a local statement, a single wire story. A small fraction become stories that many outlets in many countries keep covering. Telling these apart early is useful for triage (what should an analyst read first?) but difficult, because the signal in the first hour is sparse and noisy.

Our project, SignalRank, turns that question into a deployable system. We make four contributions: (i) a precise, leakage-free formulation of “will this event matter” with a chronological evaluation protocol; (ii) a publisher-reach prior, an out-of-fold target encoding that captures who covers an event early; (iii) an end-to-end data product covering batch and streaming ingestion, experiment tracking, a model API and a live UI; and (iv) an honest error analysis showing where early prediction fundamentally fails.

The course guidelines ask for a large dataset, data processing, model building, deployment, a front end and reproducibility; Section 5 maps each requirement to a component.

2  Related Work

GDELT was introduced by Leetaru and Schrodt [1] as a machine-coded global event database; it is widely used for conflict and protest research, but mostly for descriptive or aggregate analyses. Early prediction of popularity is a classic problem: Szabo and Huberman [2] showed that early attention to online content predicts its later popularity, and Cheng et al. [3] studied whether information cascades can be predicted from early structural and temporal features, finding the task considerably harder than predicting from an observed prefix alone. We adopt the same “early window” framing for news events and add a publisher-level prior. Target encoding for high-cardinality categories goes back to Micci-Barreca [4]; because naive encodings leak the label we use an out-of-fold variant. For modelling we use gradient boosting [5] as implemented in Spark MLlib [6], for tracking and registry MLflow [7], and for the streaming layer Spark Structured Streaming [8]. Because positives are rare we report precision–recall metrics, which are more informative than ROC curves under imbalance [9].

3  Data

GDELT 2.0 publishes three zipped, tab-delimited tables every 15 minutes: Events (who did what to whom, where; CAMEO codes, Goldstein scale, tone), Mentions (each article that mentions an event, with source name, language and tone) and the Global Knowledge Graph (themes, people, organisations and tone per article). Files follow the URL pattern data.gdeltproject.org/gdeltv2/YYYYMMDDHHMMSS.{export,mentions,gkg}, so the window is reproducible by construction.

TableFilesRaw (uncompressed)RowsKept as Parquet

GKG76810.64 GB797,087url, themes, tone
Total2,30411.49 GB (3.56 GB zipped)3.97 M0.42 GB Parquet

The GKG table dominates the volume (93%) because of its wide text fields; the project keeps only what the models need, shrinking the lake 27-fold. We join Mentions to GKG on the article URL (MentionIdentifier = DocumentIdentifier). Event time is anchored on the Events table’s DATEADDED (first appearance in GDELT); the SQLDATE field can point to earlier dates and is not used for timing. Event volume drops by about half on the weekend of 24–25 October (Figure 1), which we exploit as a natural distribution shift for testing.

4  Problem Formulation and Method

4.1  Prediction target

For each event first seen at time t0 we observe its coverage for EARLY = 60 minutes. The target is y = 1 if at least 3 new publishers, i.e. publishers not among those covering the event in the first hour, mention it between 1 h and 48 h. An earlier version of the label counted all publishers over 48 h; we dropped it because any event with five or more publishers in hour one was then positive by construction (the top three buckets of that analysis were 100% positive). The growth-based label removes this mechanical link, and the problem becomes genuinely predictive.

4.2  Features (one implementation for batch and streaming)

First-hour coverage: mentions, distinct publishers, languages, non-English mentions, distinct articles, mentions in the first 15 minutes, mean and spread of tone, mean extraction confidence and document length. Event attributes: Goldstein score, average tone, CAMEO root code, quad class, root-event flag, geographic precision, action-location and Actor1 country (top-40 values, others pooled), flags for missing actors or location. Publisher-reach prior (new): for every publisher we measure how often the events it covered in their first hour later became important, smoothed toward the global rate with strength k = 20; each event gets the mean and maximum prior of its first-hour publishers plus the share of publishers with at least five training observations. To prevent leakage, the prior of a training event is computed from the other training days only (out-of-fold by day); validation and test events use all training days. Themes: GKG themes of first-hour articles, hashed into 256 binary features (ablation).

4.3  Models and protocol

Spark MLlib logistic regression (standardised, L2) and gradient-boosted trees (40 trees, depth 5, step 0.15, 80% row subsampling) are compared with a transparent rule baseline that ranks events by first-hour publishers. Positives are up-weighted 8× during training; the decision threshold is chosen on validation data to maximise F1. The split is chronological: train 20–22 Oct (373,358 events, 6.6% positive), validation 23 Oct (117,193), test 24–25 Oct (138,903, 5.7% positive), so the test period is both unseen and a weekend. The champion is selected on validation PR-AUC only; test numbers are computed once. Confidence intervals are 95% percentile intervals from 200 bootstrap resamples of test events (paired for model differences).

Front endStreamlit “What matters now”: ranked events, map, trends, what-if scoringFigures 7–9
ReproducibilityMLflow tracking + model registry, MLproject, Makefile, Docker Compose, Airflow DAG, pinned requirementsSection 7

Streaming design. The producer publishes each 15-minute interval as JSON records to one Kafka topic. A Structured Streaming query appends every micro-batch to a rolling Parquet store; events that have accumulated 60 minutes of data time (the maximum mention timestamp seen) become “ripe”, receive features from the same early.py module used offline, are scored by the champion model and appended to the serving store that the API reads. Because it runs on data time, a replay of historical files and the live GDELT feed behave identically.

What the ablation says

The first-hour publisher count is a strong baseline (PR-AUC 0.474) and carries most of the signal (27% of GBT importance). Non-linearity helps: GBT beats logistic regression (+0.047 PR-AUC) because importance interacts with location and event type. The publisher-reach prior is the most useful addition: +0.032 PR-AUC and +0.033 F1 for GBT, with non-overlapping confidence intervals, and it also lifts logistic regression. GKG themes add nothing measurable (PR-AUC 0.586 vs 0.585; F1 is slightly lower), consistent with the idea that who covers a story early matters more than what it is about. We therefore ship the simpler model.

The champion is excellent once an event has four or more first-hour publishers (recall above 97%) but 39% of all important events begin with a single publisher, and only 4% of those are flagged: a story that breaks later, for example after an official statement, simply is not visible in hour one. We consider this a property of the problem rather than of the model, and it suggests a two-stage deployment: score at 60 minutes, re-score as coverage accumulates.

Streaming and batch agree

We replayed 12:00–17:00 on 25 October through Kafka into a separate store and compared the streaming scorer with the batch scores of the same events: of 12,202 events, first-hour publisher and mention counts matched in 100% of cases and the largest absolute score difference was 0.0. This confirms that the online path reproduces the offline features and model exactly.

7  Deployment, UI and Reproducibility

Reproducibility. make all reproduces the pipeline from raw download to evaluation: download → lake → features → prior → train → register → score → evaluate. Every training run logs parameters (feature set, class weight, split days, threshold) and metrics to MLflow; the champion is registered as signalrank-champion with alias champion and loads back through the registry URI. An MLproject file exposes the stages as MLflow entry points, docker compose up starts Kafka (KRaft mode), MLflow, the API and the dashboard, and an Airflow DAG schedules the daily batch refresh. A pytest suite (10 tests) covers the GDELT parsers, the no-look-ahead guarantee of the feature code, and the API contract (validation, batch scoring, monotonicity of the score in first-hour publishers).

8  Limitations and Ethics

Scale and window. One week of data (11.5 GB) was processed on a 2-core machine; the model has not seen seasonal variation, and the weekend test is a single, short drift check. Label definition. “Matters” is operationalised as media spread, not societal importance; heavily syndicated wire content can inflate it, and under-covered but consequential events are, by construction, missed. Publisher prior. It encodes which outlets tend to amplify stories, which can reinforce existing media visibility; its use for editorial triage should be audited for geographic and language bias, and the per-publisher table is recomputed on each retrain. Language. GDELT machine-translates sources and its coding is noisy; all conclusions inherit that noise. Streaming. The demo is a replay at accelerated speed; a live-polling mode that follows GDELT’s lastupdate.txt is implemented in the producer but was not run for the reported results, which all come from replayed intervals. The Airflow DAG was syntax-checked but not run on a scheduler.

9  Conclusion

The first hour of coverage is informative about which events will keep spreading, mostly through how many distinct publishers are already on the story, and a tree model with a leakage-safe publisher-reach prior improves on that rule by 0.111 PR-AUC and 0.057 F1 on an unseen weekend. The same code path serves batch, streaming and API scoring, and the full pipeline is reproducible from public data. The main open problem is the late bloomer: more than a third of important events are invisible at hour one, which motivates re-scoring as coverage evolves, richer content features (article text embeddings) and longer training windows as natural next steps.
